newsitem.title: USA: Russia's Mars probe not first to lose plutonium.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Mars probe not first to lose plutonium.

text.p: Sunday's crash into the South Pacific of a Russian space probe carrying plutonium raises questions about continued use of the lethal material to power or heat spacecraft, U.S. scientists said.

Three U.S. spacecraft carrying plutonium have crashed or failed since the start of the U.S. space programme, including a 1964 accident that dispersed about 100 grams of plutonium into the atmosphere 50 miles (80 km) from the Earth's surface.
The crippled Mars-96 probe lifted off from Kazakhstan's Baikonur space centre on Saturday, but failed to break out of the Earth's orbit after a booster rocket misfired.

It fell back to Earth west of Chile late Sunday, but it was not immediately clear how much of the spacecraft survived. U.S. officials said the craft was expected to burn up on reentry, but two landing vehicles were expected to survive.
Russian officials also said the four batteries, containing 200 grams of radioactive plutonium, aboard those vehicles were designed to withstand great heat and great stress on impact.
If they survived, as U.S. officials consider likely, they are probably resting on the bottom of the Pacific Ocean, which scientists see as the best possible outcome in this accident.

If they had burned up upon reentry, worst-case estimates would have pointed toward an additional 150 to 550 cancer deaths globally, although it would be impossible to ever link those deaths to this specific accident, they said.
Plutonium 238 is a very potent carcinogen that causes lung and bone cancer if inhaled.

Several scientists, including one former U.S. government official, said the latest crash raised concerns about continued use of plutonium as a heat or power source aboard probes sent into deep space, or landing vehicles.

"This incident is an occasion to reexamine the design philosophy for these power sources and even the question of their utilization in the first place," said Steven Aftergood, policy analyst with the Federation of American Scientists.

"They should minimise use of it and if there's no other way to get power, then they should go to great lengths to make sure it can survive reentry," said Frank von Hippel, a former science adviser to President Bill Clinton who is teaching public policy at Princeton University.

Von Hippel two years ago recommended improvements in the design of plutonium batteries to be used on the U.S. Cassini mission to Saturn, to be launched in October 1997, but it was too late to upgrade the encasement design for that mission.

"I was concerned about it and recommended the packaging should be improved so that we would be more confident that it would survive reentry," said von Hippel, then working in the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy.

Timothy George, the scientist at the Department of Energy's Los Alamos Laboratory who designed and tested the Cassini heat source batteries, said he had no concerns about the batteries breaking up and releasing radiation.
"They're extremely robust. I wouldn't have any qualms about heating my house with these, if someone would give them to me," George told Reuters in a telephone interview.

Tom Clements, anti-nuclear campaigner for Greenpeace USA, said there had been protests in the United States about launches involving plutonium, and this latest accident was expected to bolster opposition to its continued use.

Plutonium 238 is "perfect" for use in space because it gives off a great deal of thermal power, George said, noting that the radioactive material was in the form of ceramic pellets encapsulated in iridium or platinum rhodium alloys.
Plutonium 238 has no military uses and has a half-life of 87.5 years, much shorter than other radioactive materials that stay radioactive for thousands of years, he said.
George said the problem was that there was virtually no other way to keep spacecraft operating in deep dark space, where temperatures reach close to absolute zero.
Solar energy, which is used on U.S. Shuttle missions, does not work too close or far away from the sun.
In 1968, the U.S. Nimbus B-1 mission aborted following a launch failure, but two plutonium batteries were eventually recovered from the Pacific Ocean and reused in subsequent flights.
Plutonium batteries aboard a lunar lander jettisoned from the 1970 mission Apollo 13 presumably went into the Pacific Ocean as well, but have never been recovered.
